2.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux map is inferred from the consistency of
atom transitions with the measured isotopomer distribution in a network that
is at metabolic and isotopic steady state.

The core mathematical objects of an INST-MFA / SS 13C-MFA are therefore

* the network stoichiometry with atom mappings, i.e. a stoichiometric matrix
  N and the atom transition network that maps the carbon atoms of
  substrates to products,
  1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry;

  The stoichiometry defines the mass balance constraints

  N . v = 0

  at metabolic steady state and the isotopomer balance constraints

  f(v, X) = Xmeas

  at isotopic steady state.  No kinetic rate laws are used.

* the experimental isotopomer/ mass isotopomer distribution data that
  make the flux problem identifiable,
  6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates.

  Measured MID / flux isotopomer distributions from MS/NMR are the data
  to which the predicted labelling pattern from the atom transition model
  is fitted.

That is all that is strictly required for the 13C-MFA isotopomer equations.
Maximum cell density in a bioreactor 2., enzyme kinetics 4. and regulatory
network information 5. are not used in a steady-state flux balance / 
isotopomer balance formulation; a kinetic or regulatory model is a
different modelling level.

In practice the metabolic network is closed with a biomass drain.  Closing
the network requires a definition of the biomass reaction, i.e. the
fractional composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. and the
corresponding precursor drains, 3. Biomass composition of the organism.
It is therefore normally supplied together with the stoichiometric model
to obtain a physically meaningful, closed flux distribution and to relate
the measured growth rate/extracellular rates to intracellular fluxes, but
the atom-mapping / MID fitting equations themselves require only the
stoichiometry and the measured labelling.  If the biomass reaction is
counted as a separate piece of information the commonly quoted practical
set is 1, 3 and 6, i.e. 3/6 items, 1 and 6 being the strictly essential
13C-MFA data.

4.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
stoichiometric / atom-transition constraints of the network together
with the experimentally measured isotopic constraints, and the flux
solution is obtained by non-linear fitting of the simulated mass
isotopomer distributions to the measured ones. No kinetic or regulatory
information is used and the problem is strictly stoichiometric /
isotopomeric.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Yes. The stoichiometric matrix S
and, for 13C, the atom mapping / atom transition network that links
the carbon atoms of substrates and products is the structural model on
which the flux balance S·v = 0 and the isotopomer balance equations are
built. In practice the stoichiometric model is the one that contains the
central carbon network and the biomass drain reaction.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Yes. Steady
state 13C-MFA is an inverse problem. The measured mass isotopomer
distributions, MIDs, of intracellular – and usually also extracellular –
metabolites, obtained by GC-MS/LC-MS/NMR after growth on a defined
13C labelled tracer, provide the isotopic constraints that make the
network identifiable. Together with the independent extracellular
exchange fluxes the MIDs are fitted to the fluxes v predicted from the
atom transition model.

That is the minimal information set for a classical steady state 13C-MFA.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor is not needed for
the flux calculation. Cell density is a process parameter; what is needed,
if any, is the specific uptake/secretion rates, i.e. the extracellular
fluxes normalized to biomass or volume, not a maximum attainable density.

4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used. Steady state
13C-MFA is a constraint-based, non-kinetic method. Kinetic constants
and regulatory wiring affect the value of the fluxes but they are not
required to solve the stoichiometric + isotopomeric problem.

3. Biomass composition. Strictly speaking the isotopic fitting does not
require an a priori biomass composition; the biomass drain can be left
as an unknown sink and the fluxes in the core network are determined by
stoichiometry + MIDs. In routine practice the biomass reaction is
written explicitly and its stoichiometric coefficients are derived from
the measured/assumed fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. so the
composition is commonly used to close the model and to express the
biomass formation rate. If the biomass reaction is counted as part of the
network stoichiometry the composition is the usual practical third input.
Apart from that formal requirement it is not a kinetic/regulatory input.

Hence on a formal level the strictly essential inputs from the list are
1 and 6, two of the six items, the stoichiometric/atom-transition model
and the measured 13C labelling patterns. With the conventional
closure of the biomass drain the biomass composition is the third
practically required piece of information.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3

For a steady-state 13C-MFA the core constraints are the network structure and the measured isotope data, plus a definition of the biomass sink.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required to write the atom-mapping and mass balance equations that relate fluxes to the labeling of intermediates.
6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, typically from MS or NMR measurements of proteinogenic amino acids or intracellular metabolites, provide the isotopomer constraints that allow the flux ratios to be resolved.

3. Biomass composition of the organism, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, is also needed in practice to define the biomass formation reaction and the precursor drain stoichiometry. Without a defined biomass composition the network is not closed and absolute fluxes cannot be anchored to growth.

Maximum cell density in a bioreactor, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used in the steady-state isotopomer balance formulation; they are relevant for dynamic modelling or kinetic flux estimation but not for conventional 13C-MFA.

6.text:
For an isotopic steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
isotopomer balance equations together with the network mass balance

S . v = 0  ,   M(v) . x = x

where S is the network stoichiometric matrix, v the flux vector and x the
vector of measured mass isotopomer / fractional labelling distributions.
In the isotopomer formalism the only data that enter the data-fitting
problem are

* the atom transition / reaction stoichiometry of the network that is
used to build the stoichiometric matrix S and the carbon atom mapping
M(v) for every reaction, and
* the experimental labelling data, i.e. the mass isotopomer or 13C
fractional labelling patterns of the intracellular – and of the
extracellular – metabolites that can be measured by MS/NMR.

Hence in the strict isotopic sense

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry - required.  S and the atom maps
are needed to relate a given flux distribution to the labelling
patterns that will be observed. 

6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates - required.
The 13C labelling data are the experimental observations that the
flux distribution has to reproduce.

That is the information that is used in the actual isotopomer
optimization.  In particular a 13C-MFA at metabolic steady state is
thermodynamic/isotopomer based and does not need kinetic parameters,
knowledge of regulation and it does not need a bioprocess parameter
such as the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – not required
for the isotopic flux determination. It is a process / scale up
parameter.
4. Enzyme kinetics – not required. 13C-MFA is a steady state,
non kinetic method.
5. Regulatory networks – not required for the isotopomer calculation.

The biomass composition is normally used in practice to write the
biomass drain reaction that closes the network and to convert a measured
growth rate into a carbon demand for biomass formation, i.e. to build the
stoichiometric entry for biomass in item 1.  Once the network, including
a biomass reaction, is written as a stoichiometric matrix the
isotopomer problem itself needs only the stoichiometry and the labelling
data.  If the need to be able to construct a closed biomass reaction is
counted as a separate input the model build is often quoted as
stoichiometry + biomass composition + labelling, i.e. three of the six
items listed.

8.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the best fit of a
stoichiometric model to the measured isotope data and not from kinetics
or gene regulation.

The mathematical core of the problem is

* v = 0  ,  S v = 0  steady state mass balance
* dX/dt = 0 ,  X = f(S, v, c0)  steady state labelling balance

where S is the stoichiometric matrix, v the unknown internal fluxes
and X the predicted fractional labelling of the metabolite pools.
That needs

* the network stoichiometry, i.e. the reaction list and the atom
transition mappings which define how the carbon atoms are carried
through the network. This is item 1. The stoichiometric network is
the only mechanistic information that enters the mass- and the
labelling-balance equations.
* the experimental isotopic data that constrain the v’s. In practice
the fractional 13C labelling patterns of proteinogenic amino acids
or of free intracellular intermediates measured by MS/NMR, and the
known labelling of the supplied carbon source. This is item 6.

The fit is independent of enzyme kinetics, of regulatory networks and
of the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor. Items 2, 4 and 5
are therefore not required for the 13C-MFA per se.

In a fully closed implementation the biomass drain is written as a
stoichiometric reaction. The coefficients of that biomass reaction are
obtained from the measured biomass composition, i.e. the fraction of
protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. and the growth rate, item 3. Once
the biomass reaction is written it is formally part of the
stoichiometric matrix S. If the biomass reaction is taken as given,
the strictly indispensable experimental inputs for the steady state
13C-MFA are the stoichiometry and the intracellular labelling
patterns, items 1 and 6, two items. With the usual closed network
formalism the biomass composition required to define the biomass sink
is the third practically required piece of information, items 1,3 and
6.

10.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are inferred from the relationship

flux → atom transitions → isotopomer / mass isotopomer distributions

which is a purely stoichiometric / atom-mapping problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required. The network and the carbon atom transitions in each reaction define the isotopomer mapping function that relates a set of fluxes v to the predicted labelling patterns of the intracellular pools. The stoichiometric matrix is also needed for the steady state mass balance Sv = 0.
* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is required. The measured 13C mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular metabolites, normally obtained by GC-MS / NMR after a 13C tracer experiment at isotopic steady state, are the experimental constraints that the flux vector has to reproduce. Together with 1. they define the non-linear least squares problem min_v || MID_measured - MID_predicted(v) ||.

The method is flux-omics and it is completely kinetic free.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in 13C-MFA. 13C-MFA is made at metabolic and isotopic steady state and is independent of the kinetics and regulation that generate the steady state and independent of the absolute scale of the culture. The scale is set by measured specific uptake / secretion rates, not by a maximal achievable density.

In practice the biomass drain is normally written explicitly in the stoichiometric model and that is where 3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. the fractional amounts of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, nucleic acid etc. is used, to define the biomass formation reaction and the mapping of label into biomass precursors. In the minimal formal formulation the biomass reaction is part of the stoichiometry in 1., so the strictly essential experimental inputs are the network stoichiometry and the intracellular 13C labelling data, i.e. 2 items, 1 and 6. With the conventional explicit biomass equation the practical data set is stoichiometry, biomass composition and the intracellular MID data, i.e. items 1, 3 and 6, three items in the list as written.

12.text:
In a strictly isotopomer based steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained
from the mapping of a labelled carbon skeleton through a defined network.

The two pieces of information that are mathematically indispensable are

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry and the carbon atom transitions
  that go with it. The atom mapping defines the isotopomer balance
  equations

  dX/dt = S v + T X  = 0 at isotopic steady state

  and the ordinary stoichiometric balances S v = 0 which are used to
  eliminate dependent fluxes. Without a stoichiometric network and an
  atom mapping the labeling patterns cannot be translated into fluxes.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. The
  measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. from GC-MS / NMR of
  proteinogenic amino acids or free intracellular metabolites, are the
  experimental constraints that make the flux distribution identifiable.
  The labeling data together with the atom mapping give the
  13C-constraints for v.

That is the minimal information content of 13C-MFA. Extracellular
uptake/secretion rates and a growth rate are in practice measured and
used as additional constraints, but they are not part of the six items
listed.

Maximal cell density in a bioreactor, enzyme kinetics and regulatory
networks are kinetic / physiological descriptors. They are not required
for the isotopomer balance formulation and the steady state 13C-MFA
solution is independent of them.

2. Maximum cell density is not used for the flux calculation.
4. Enzyme kinetics is not used, 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric /
isotopomer – not a kinetic – method.
5. Regulatory networks are not used.

In the usual practical implementation the network is closed with a
biomass drain reaction. To build the biomass drain and to convert a
measured specific growth rate into molar precursor demands for protein,
lipid, carbohydrate, etc. the biomass composition

3. Biomass composition of the organism

is routinely supplied. With that closure the practically used set is
1, 3 and 6, stoichiometry + atom mapping, measured labeling patterns
and a defined biomass reaction, i.e. the two strictly essential items
1 and 6, commonly quoted as the three items 1, 3 and 6. The kinetic and
regulatory items 2, 4 and 5 remain unnecessary for steady state
13C-MFA.

1.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the coupling of
mass balance and isotope balance on the network

v . S = 0          mass steady state
v . Siso = 0       isotopic steady state

Hence you need a network with defined atom transitions and you need an
experimental isotopic constraint that can be used in the isotope balance.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry.  Yes. 
The stoichiometric matrix S and the atom-mapping for every reaction in
the model is needed to write the mass balances and the carbon-atom
transition equations that couple the labelling of the precursors to the
labelling of the products.  The biomass formation reaction is part of
that stoichiometric description.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates.  Yes.
In the steady state the measured 13C-enrichment pattern of the
intracellular metabolites, essentially proteinogenic amino acids as
proxies for the central carbon intermediates, is the experimental
constraint that allows the isotopic steady state equations to be solved
for the flux distribution v.  The extracellular 13C-substrate labelling
is also required in practice.

The other items are not required for a classic steady state 13C-MFA.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No. Cell
density per se is not used in the isotopic balances. Specific uptake/
secretion rates are needed, but the maximal achievable density is not.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No.  13C-MFA is a stoichiometric / isotopic
constraint problem. Kinetic rate laws and kinetic parameters are not
used in the steady state formulation.

* 5. Regulatory networks. No. Regulation is not needed to solve the
stoichiometric + isotopic balances.

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism.  In practice yes, as the
practical closure of the network. The stoichiometry of the biomass
formation/drain reaction is normally built from the measured fractional
composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, RNA, DNA, etc., so that
the network is mass balanced and the carbon fluxes that leave the
central metabolism to biomass can be written.  Formally this is part of
the stoichiometric description of the network. With the biomass
reaction supplied externally the absolute minimal core of a steady state
13C-MFA is therefore

stoichiometry + atom mapping + measured 13C labelling

i.e. items 1 and 6, three items in the list as written if the biomass
reaction is counted explicitly as item 3.  If biomass composition is
taken as part of the stoichiometric model the irreducible core is
stoichiometry and isotopic labelling, i.e. 2 of the 6 listed items.

5.text:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
isotopomer balances

    S . v = 0
    M( v ) . x = 0

on a network with known atom transitions. That is all that is formally
required for the isotopomer part of the problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with atom mapping.  Yes.  The
stoichiometric matrix S and the atom transition matrix M for every
reaction in the network that is to be used in the fit are mandatory.
Without a defined network with known carbon atom transitions no
isotopomer balance can be written.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates.  Yes.  The
measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. from proteinogenic amino
acids, intracellular free metabolites by MS/NMR, etc., are the data
that constrain the fluxes in the 13C model.  In practice the
extracellular specific uptake / secretion rates that are needed to
close the mass balances are also measured, i.e. a growth rate and
medium consumption/production.

The remaining items are not part of a steady-state 13C-MFA:

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No.  Cell
density is a scale up / process parameter. Fluxes are expressed on a
per biomass or per cell basis and are independent of the absolute
bioreactor density.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No.  Steady state MFA is a stoichiometric/
isotopomer constrained estimation. Kinetic parameters are not used
in the 13C-MFA formulation and are not required for the flux
identifiability.

* 5. Regulatory networks. No.  Regulation is not used in the
stoichiometric/isotopomer balances.

* 3. Biomass composition.  Strictly speaking the isotopomer model
does not need the elemental composition of protein, lipid and
carbohydrate. The biomass can be taken as a black box drain of the
precursor metabolites that are measured. In practice a closed
stoichiometric model is usually written with an explicit biomass
reaction

    Biomass = sum_i c_i M_i

and then the c_i are the biomass composition coefficients.  If a fully
closed network with a defined biomass sink is wanted the composition
is used to define that sink, so that in a textbook presentation the
set 1 + 3 + 6 is quoted as the minimal information for a closed
steady-state 13C-MFA. The core isotopomer information is 1 and 6.

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In a conventional steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes v are obtained from
the stoichiometric mass balance

S·v = 0

together with the isotopomer / labeling balance constraints which are
obtained from the measured 13C enrichments. Nothing kinetic / regulatory
is involved and the absolute scale of the culture, e.g. the maximal
bioreactor cell density, is irrelevant for the flux distribution per
C-mol biomass.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry – required. The stoichiometric
matrix S and the atom transition maps that underlie the isotopomer
balance equations are the model. Without S no mass balance can be written
and no labelling propagation can be defined.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates – required.
The experimental constraints for MFA are the measured 13C enrichments
of intracellular, or proteinogenic, metabolites, usually expressed as
mass isotopomer distributions or MID’s. The MID’s together with S give
the non-linear labelling balance equations that resolve the otherwise
underdetermined linear system S·v = 0.

Enzyme kinetics 4. and regulatory networks 5. are not used in a
steady-state MFA. The fluxes are obtained from stoichiometry plus
labelling constraints, not from v = f(E,Km,kcat) nor from gene
regulation. Maximum cell density 2. of the bioreactor is a scale
factor and is not a constraint for the relative flux distribution.

In practice the stoichiometric model is closed with a biomass
formation reaction. The coefficients of that drain are normally written
in terms of the macromolecular composition of the organism, i.e. the
fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. that makes up the biomass.
Hence biomass composition 3. is routinely required to define the
biomass sink that closes the carbon, redox and degree-of-reduction
balances and to convert a measured growth rate into a C-mol biomass
demand. With the biomass reaction included the routinely used inputs
are therefore 1, 3 and 6. If the biomass drain is taken as a generic
lumped sink the minimal, formally independent, inputs for 13C-MFA are
the stoichiometric network 1 and the measured 13C labelling patterns 6,
i.e. two items in the list.

11.text:
In a formal 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the stoichiometric
consequences of the network and from the measured mass isotopomer
distributions, under the steady state assumption dC/dt = 0 , dX/dt = 0.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry - yes.  The stoichiometric matrix
N v = 0 together with the atom transition mappings for every reaction
is the structural part of the model on which the isotopomer balances

    dX/dt = f(v,X) = 0

are written. Without a defined network the isotopomer balances cannot
be formulated.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates - yes.
The measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. of proteinogenic
amino acids / intracellular metabolites that are the experimental
read-out of the 13C-labelling experiment, are the data that constrain
the flux distribution v. The MFA problem is

    minimise || Xmeas - Xcalc(v) ||  s.t.  N v = 0 

so the labeling data are the essential experimental input.

The other items are not part of the steady state 13C-MFA formulation.

* 2. Maximum cell density in a bioreactor - not required.  Cell density
is a scale-up / bioprocess parameter. Fluxes are expressed in
mmol gDW-1 h-1 or specific rates and are independent of the absolute
biomass that can be reached in a bioreactor.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics - not required.  MFA is stoichiometric /
isotopomer based. Kinetic constants, Vmax/Km etc., are needed for
kinetic or dynamic flux modelling but not for a steady state
isotopomer based flux estimation.

* 5. Regulatory networks - not required.  Regulation can be used to
reduce the solution space a posteriori but it is not a formal
requirement for the 13C-MFA equations.

* 3. Biomass composition - not a formal requirement of the MFA
equations themselves.  It is routinely used in practice to write an
explicit biomass drain reaction and to close carbon/nitrogen balances
and to convert a measured growth rate into a specific biomass
formation flux.  In the strict stoichiometric + isotopomer formulation
the biomass sink can be introduced as a measured specific growth rate
with an unspecified composition.  If a fully closed network with an
explicit biomass reaction is required in practice the biomass
composition is the third practical input in addition to 1 and 6.

Hence from the list as written the formal, indispensable MFA inputs are
stoichiometry and the measured 13C labelling patterns, i.e. 2 of the 6
items, 1 and 6.  With the usual practical closure of the model the
biomass composition is also brought in, giving the commonly quoted
three practical inputs: stoichiometry, biomass composition and isotopic
labelling.

9.text:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained
by fitting an isotopomer / cumomer model to measured labeling data under
steady state mass balance constraints.

The core of the method is

* a defined metabolic network with atom mappings,
 i.e. the reaction stoichiometry and the carbon transitions which link
 substrate atoms to product atoms. The stoichiometry provides the
 mass balances 

    S . v =0

and the atom transitions which are used to build the isotopomer
balance equations. Kinetic parameters and the regulatory state of the
network are not entered in the isotopomer balance.

* the experimental 13C labeling pattern of the intracellular
metabolic intermediates, usually obtained by GC-MS / LC-MS/MS after
steady state labeling with [U-13C] glucose or other tracers, and the
corresponding extracellular flux rates which are used to scale the
model. The labeling data are the only experimentally observed
quantities which break the stoichiometric degree of freedom of the
network.

In particular maximum cell density in the bioreactor, enzyme
kinetics and the regulatory network are not used in steady state
13C-MFA. The maximum cell density is a process / scale up parameter
and kinetics / regulation are not required for a stoichiometric/
isotopomer fit.

In practice the network is closed with a biomass formation reaction.
Writing that reaction needs the macromolecular biomass composition,
protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc., i.e. the stoichiometric coefficients
of the precursors that are drained to growth. Once the biomass
reaction is written it is part of the stoichiometric model. Strictly
speaking the isotopomer fit therefore needs

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry,
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates,

and, in the usual implementation, the biomass stoichiometry which is
specified by 3. Biomass composition of the organism. Items 2. Maximum
cell density, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not
required for steady state 13C-MFA.

If the biomass reaction is taken as given within item 1 the minimal
information set is stoichiometry + labeling, i.e. two of the six listed
items, 1 and 6. With the conventional explicit biomass formulation this
is normally quoted as the three items 1, 3 and 6, 2, 4 and 5 being
unnecessary.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3

For a steady-state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained from mass balance constraints plus the information contained in the measured isotopomers. That needs:

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, to write the atom mappings and the stoichiometric mass balance equations for each metabolite at steady state, dC/dt = 0.

6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, which are the experimental data that constrain the fractional contributions of different precursor pools to each metabolite and therefore the flux split ratios.

3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates. The biomass drain must be represented as a pseudo-reaction in the network. Its stoichiometry, and therefore the carbon demand that closes the network, is defined by the measured biomass composition. Without a defined biomass reaction you cannot enforce carbon and redox closure and the labeling of the biomass precursors cannot be properly accounted for.

Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not required for the isotopic steady-state calculation. The fluxes are inferred from stoichiometry and isotopomer balancing, not from kinetic parameters, regulation or culture scale.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3 items are required, namely 1, 3 and 6.

Stoichiometry is essential to build the atom transition matrix and the mass balance equations that define the network topology at steady state. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the flux solution in 13C-MFA; without measured mass isotopomer distributions there is no way to resolve flux splits.

Biomass composition is also needed in practice to define a proper biomass drain reaction. In a steady-state 13C-MFA the network has to be closed and the carbon fate to biomass must be accounted for, which is done via a biomass equation constructed from the measured fractions of protein, lipids and carbohydrates and the corresponding average amino acid, fatty acid and sugar compositions. That closes the mass balance and allows conversion of relative fluxes to absolute fluxes. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used for the stoichiometric + isotopomer balancing that underlies steady-state 13C-MFA.

3.text:
In a steady-state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the consistency of a
stoichiometric / atom-transition model with experimentally measured isotopomer
distributions. The kinetic / regulatory description of the network is not used
and the culture scale is not used.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry : required. The atom mapping of the
network, i.e. the reaction stoichiometry together with the carbon atom
transitions, is the structural model on which the isotopomer balances are
written. Without a defined network the labelling data cannot be mapped onto
flux ratios.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates : required.
The measured 13C enrichment of intracellular intermediates, in practice
usually of proteinogenic amino acids derived from the intracellular
metabolite pool, is the experimental constraint that makes the flux ratios
identifiable. Steady state 13C-MFA is the joint solution of
S.v = 0 and of the isotopomer balance equations
v → MID

* 4. Enzyme kinetics, 5. Regulatory networks and 2. Maximum cell density of
the organism in a bioreactor are not required for the isotopic
constraint based calculation. Steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric /
isotopomer method and is independent of kinetic parameters, regulation
and of the absolute scale of cultivation.

In practice absolute fluxes are obtained only after the isotopic flux
ratios are scaled to an absolute scale, e.g. by a measured specific growth
rate and a defined biomass formation reaction. The biomass formation
reaction is normally written from the measured biomass composition, i.e.
the fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., so that the drain of
precursor metabolites to biomass can be closed in the stoichiometric model.
With the usual textbook complete model this is the third piece of
information that is used together with 1 and 6, i.e. stoichiometry +
biomass composition + labelling data.

If the scaling is taken as given the strictly isotopic essentials are the
two listed items 1 and 6, stoichiometry + measured 13C labelling patterns.
That is the 2-item core of 13C-MFA, routinely quoted as 3 items in the
practical implementation 1,3 and 6.

* the experimental isotopomer/ mass isotopomer distribution data that

  6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates.

It is therefore normally supplied together with the stoichiometric model
to obtain a physically meaningful, closed flux distribution and to relate
the measured growth rate/extracellular rates to intracellular fluxes, but
the atom-mapping / MID fitting equations themselves require only the
stoichiometry and the measured labelling.  If the biomass reaction is
counted as a separate piece of information the commonly quoted practical
set is 1, 3 and 6, i.e. 3/6 items, 1 and 6 being the strictly essential
13C-MFA data.
public_text.4:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
stoichiometric / atom-transition constraints of the network together
with the experimentally measured isotopic constraints, and the flux
solution is obtained by non-linear fitting of the simulated mass
isotopomer distributions to the measured ones. No kinetic or regulatory
information is used and the problem is strictly stoichiometric /
isotopomeric.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Yes. The stoichiometric matrix S
and, for 13C, the atom mapping / atom transition network that links
the carbon atoms of substrates and products is the structural model on
which the flux balance S·v = 0 and the isotopomer balance equations are
built. In practice the stoichiometric model is the one that contains the
central carbon network and the biomass drain reaction.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Yes. Steady
state 13C-MFA is an inverse problem. The measured mass isotopomer
distributions, MIDs, of intracellular – and usually also extracellular –
metabolites, obtained by GC-MS/LC-MS/NMR after growth on a defined
13C labelled tracer, provide the isotopic constraints that make the
network identifiable. Together with the independent extracellular
exchange fluxes the MIDs are fitted to the fluxes v predicted from the
atom transition model.

That is the minimal information set for a classical steady state 13C-MFA.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor is not needed for
the flux calculation. Cell density is a process parameter; what is needed,
if any, is the specific uptake/secretion rates, i.e. the extracellular
fluxes normalized to biomass or volume, not a maximum attainable density.

4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used. Steady state
13C-MFA is a constraint-based, non-kinetic method. Kinetic constants
and regulatory wiring affect the value of the fluxes but they are not
required to solve the stoichiometric + isotopomeric problem.

3. Biomass composition. Strictly speaking the isotopic fitting does not
require an a priori biomass composition; the biomass drain can be left
as an unknown sink and the fluxes in the core network are determined by
stoichiometry + MIDs. In routine practice the biomass reaction is
written explicitly and its stoichiometric coefficients are derived from
the measured/assumed fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. so the
composition is commonly used to close the model and to express the
biomass formation rate. If the biomass reaction is counted as part of the
network stoichiometry the composition is the usual practical third input.
Apart from that formal requirement it is not a kinetic/regulatory input.

Hence on a formal level the strictly essential inputs from the list are
1 and 6, two of the six items, the stoichiometric/atom-transition model
and the measured 13C labelling patterns. With the conventional
closure of the biomass drain the biomass composition is the third
practically required piece of information.
public_text.14:
3

For a steady-state 13C-MFA the core constraints are the network structure and the measured isotope data, plus a definition of the biomass sink.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required to write the atom-mapping and mass balance equations that relate fluxes to the labeling of intermediates.
6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, typically from MS or NMR measurements of proteinogenic amino acids or intracellular metabolites, provide the isotopomer constraints that allow the flux ratios to be resolved.

3. Biomass composition of the organism, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates, is also needed in practice to define the biomass formation reaction and the precursor drain stoichiometry. Without a defined biomass composition the network is not closed and absolute fluxes cannot be anchored to growth.

Maximum cell density in a bioreactor, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used in the steady-state isotopomer balance formulation; they are relevant for dynamic modelling or kinetic flux estimation but not for conventional 13C-MFA.
public_text.6:
For an isotopic steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
isotopomer balance equations together with the network mass balance

S . v = 0  ,   M(v) . x = x

where S is the network stoichiometric matrix, v the flux vector and x the
vector of measured mass isotopomer / fractional labelling distributions.
In the isotopomer formalism the only data that enter the data-fitting
problem are

* the atom transition / reaction stoichiometry of the network that is
used to build the stoichiometric matrix S and the carbon atom mapping
M(v) for every reaction, and
* the experimental labelling data, i.e. the mass isotopomer or 13C
fractional labelling patterns of the intracellular – and of the
extracellular – metabolites that can be measured by MS/NMR.

Hence in the strict isotopic sense

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry - required.  S and the atom maps
are needed to relate a given flux distribution to the labelling
patterns that will be observed. 

6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates - required.
The 13C labelling data are the experimental observations that the
flux distribution has to reproduce.

That is the information that is used in the actual isotopomer
optimization.  In particular a 13C-MFA at metabolic steady state is
thermodynamic/isotopomer based and does not need kinetic parameters,
knowledge of regulation and it does not need a bioprocess parameter
such as the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – not required
for the isotopic flux determination. It is a process / scale up
parameter.
4. Enzyme kinetics – not required. 13C-MFA is a steady state,
non kinetic method.
5. Regulatory networks – not required for the isotopomer calculation.

The biomass composition is normally used in practice to write the
biomass drain reaction that closes the network and to convert a measured
growth rate into a carbon demand for biomass formation, i.e. to build the
stoichiometric entry for biomass in item 1.  Once the network, including
a biomass reaction, is written as a stoichiometric matrix the
isotopomer problem itself needs only the stoichiometry and the labelling
data.  If the need to be able to construct a closed biomass reaction is
counted as a separate input the model build is often quoted as
stoichiometry + biomass composition + labelling, i.e. three of the six
items listed.
public_text.8:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the best fit of a
stoichiometric model to the measured isotope data and not from kinetics
or gene regulation.

The mathematical core of the problem is

* v = 0  ,  S v = 0  steady state mass balance
* dX/dt = 0 ,  X = f(S, v, c0)  steady state labelling balance

where S is the stoichiometric matrix, v the unknown internal fluxes
and X the predicted fractional labelling of the metabolite pools.
That needs

* the network stoichiometry, i.e. the reaction list and the atom
transition mappings which define how the carbon atoms are carried
through the network. This is item 1. The stoichiometric network is
the only mechanistic information that enters the mass- and the
labelling-balance equations.
* the experimental isotopic data that constrain the v’s. In practice
the fractional 13C labelling patterns of proteinogenic amino acids
or of free intracellular intermediates measured by MS/NMR, and the
known labelling of the supplied carbon source. This is item 6.

The fit is independent of enzyme kinetics, of regulatory networks and
of the maximum attainable cell density in a bioreactor. Items 2, 4 and 5
are therefore not required for the 13C-MFA per se.

In a fully closed implementation the biomass drain is written as a
stoichiometric reaction. The coefficients of that biomass reaction are
obtained from the measured biomass composition, i.e. the fraction of
protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. and the growth rate, item 3. Once
the biomass reaction is written it is formally part of the
stoichiometric matrix S. If the biomass reaction is taken as given,
the strictly indispensable experimental inputs for the steady state
13C-MFA are the stoichiometry and the intracellular labelling
patterns, items 1 and 6, two items. With the usual closed network
formalism the biomass composition required to define the biomass sink
is the third practically required piece of information, items 1,3 and
6.
public_text.10:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are inferred from the relationship

flux → atom transitions → isotopomer / mass isotopomer distributions

which is a purely stoichiometric / atom-mapping problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required. The network and the carbon atom transitions in each reaction define the isotopomer mapping function that relates a set of fluxes v to the predicted labelling patterns of the intracellular pools. The stoichiometric matrix is also needed for the steady state mass balance Sv = 0.
* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is required. The measured 13C mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular metabolites, normally obtained by GC-MS / NMR after a 13C tracer experiment at isotopic steady state, are the experimental constraints that the flux vector has to reproduce. Together with 1. they define the non-linear least squares problem min_v || MID_measured - MID_predicted(v) ||.

The method is flux-omics and it is completely kinetic free.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in 13C-MFA. 13C-MFA is made at metabolic and isotopic steady state and is independent of the kinetics and regulation that generate the steady state and independent of the absolute scale of the culture. The scale is set by measured specific uptake / secretion rates, not by a maximal achievable density.

In practice the biomass drain is normally written explicitly in the stoichiometric model and that is where 3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. the fractional amounts of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, nucleic acid etc. is used, to define the biomass formation reaction and the mapping of label into biomass precursors. In the minimal formal formulation the biomass reaction is part of the stoichiometry in 1., so the strictly essential experimental inputs are the network stoichiometry and the intracellular 13C labelling data, i.e. 2 items, 1 and 6. With the conventional explicit biomass equation the practical data set is stoichiometry, biomass composition and the intracellular MID data, i.e. items 1, 3 and 6, three items in the list as written.
public_text.12:
In a strictly isotopomer based steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained
from the mapping of a labelled carbon skeleton through a defined network.

The two pieces of information that are mathematically indispensable are

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry and the carbon atom transitions
  that go with it. The atom mapping defines the isotopomer balance
  equations

  dX/dt = S v + T X  = 0 at isotopic steady state

  and the ordinary stoichiometric balances S v = 0 which are used to
  eliminate dependent fluxes. Without a stoichiometric network and an
  atom mapping the labeling patterns cannot be translated into fluxes.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. The
  measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. from GC-MS / NMR of
  proteinogenic amino acids or free intracellular metabolites, are the
  experimental constraints that make the flux distribution identifiable.
  The labeling data together with the atom mapping give the
  13C-constraints for v.

That is the minimal information content of 13C-MFA. Extracellular
uptake/secretion rates and a growth rate are in practice measured and
used as additional constraints, but they are not part of the six items
listed.

Maximal cell density in a bioreactor, enzyme kinetics and regulatory
networks are kinetic / physiological descriptors. They are not required
for the isotopomer balance formulation and the steady state 13C-MFA
solution is independent of them.

2. Maximum cell density is not used for the flux calculation.
4. Enzyme kinetics is not used, 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric /
isotopomer – not a kinetic – method.
5. Regulatory networks are not used.

In the usual practical implementation the network is closed with a
biomass drain reaction. To build the biomass drain and to convert a
measured specific growth rate into molar precursor demands for protein,
lipid, carbohydrate, etc. the biomass composition

3. Biomass composition of the organism

is routinely supplied. With that closure the practically used set is
1, 3 and 6, stoichiometry + atom mapping, measured labeling patterns
and a defined biomass reaction, i.e. the two strictly essential items
1 and 6, commonly quoted as the three items 1, 3 and 6. The kinetic and
regulatory items 2, 4 and 5 remain unnecessary for steady state
13C-MFA.
public_text.1:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the coupling of
mass balance and isotope balance on the network

v . S = 0          mass steady state
v . Siso = 0       isotopic steady state

Hence you need a network with defined atom transitions and you need an
experimental isotopic constraint that can be used in the isotope balance.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry.  Yes. 
The stoichiometric matrix S and the atom-mapping for every reaction in
the model is needed to write the mass balances and the carbon-atom
transition equations that couple the labelling of the precursors to the
labelling of the products.  The biomass formation reaction is part of
that stoichiometric description.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates.  Yes.
In the steady state the measured 13C-enrichment pattern of the
intracellular metabolites, essentially proteinogenic amino acids as
proxies for the central carbon intermediates, is the experimental
constraint that allows the isotopic steady state equations to be solved
for the flux distribution v.  The extracellular 13C-substrate labelling
is also required in practice.

The other items are not required for a classic steady state 13C-MFA.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No. Cell
density per se is not used in the isotopic balances. Specific uptake/
secretion rates are needed, but the maximal achievable density is not.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No.  13C-MFA is a stoichiometric / isotopic
constraint problem. Kinetic rate laws and kinetic parameters are not
used in the steady state formulation.

* 5. Regulatory networks. No. Regulation is not needed to solve the
stoichiometric + isotopic balances.

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism.  In practice yes, as the
practical closure of the network. The stoichiometry of the biomass
formation/drain reaction is normally built from the measured fractional
composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, RNA, DNA, etc., so that
the network is mass balanced and the carbon fluxes that leave the
central metabolism to biomass can be written.  Formally this is part of
the stoichiometric description of the network. With the biomass
reaction supplied externally the absolute minimal core of a steady state
13C-MFA is therefore

stoichiometry + atom mapping + measured 13C labelling

i.e. items 1 and 6, three items in the list as written if the biomass
reaction is counted explicitly as item 3.  If biomass composition is
taken as part of the stoichiometric model the irreducible core is
stoichiometry and isotopic labelling, i.e. 2 of the 6 listed items.
public_text.5:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
isotopomer balances

    S . v = 0
    M( v ) . x = 0

on a network with known atom transitions. That is all that is formally
required for the isotopomer part of the problem.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with atom mapping.  Yes.  The
stoichiometric matrix S and the atom transition matrix M for every
reaction in the network that is to be used in the fit are mandatory.
Without a defined network with known carbon atom transitions no
isotopomer balance can be written.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates.  Yes.  The
measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. from proteinogenic amino
acids, intracellular free metabolites by MS/NMR, etc., are the data
that constrain the fluxes in the 13C model.  In practice the
extracellular specific uptake / secretion rates that are needed to
close the mass balances are also measured, i.e. a growth rate and
medium consumption/production.

The remaining items are not part of a steady-state 13C-MFA:

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No.  Cell
density is a scale up / process parameter. Fluxes are expressed on a
per biomass or per cell basis and are independent of the absolute
bioreactor density.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No.  Steady state MFA is a stoichiometric/
isotopomer constrained estimation. Kinetic parameters are not used
in the 13C-MFA formulation and are not required for the flux
identifiability.

* 5. Regulatory networks. No.  Regulation is not used in the
stoichiometric/isotopomer balances.

* 3. Biomass composition.  Strictly speaking the isotopomer model
does not need the elemental composition of protein, lipid and
carbohydrate. The biomass can be taken as a black box drain of the
precursor metabolites that are measured. In practice a closed
stoichiometric model is usually written with an explicit biomass
reaction

    Biomass = sum_i c_i M_i

and then the c_i are the biomass composition coefficients.  If a fully
closed network with a defined biomass sink is wanted the composition
is used to define that sink, so that in a textbook presentation the
set 1 + 3 + 6 is quoted as the minimal information for a closed
steady-state 13C-MFA. The core isotopomer information is 1 and 6.
public_text.15:
In a conventional steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes v are obtained from
the stoichiometric mass balance

S·v = 0

together with the isotopomer / labeling balance constraints which are
obtained from the measured 13C enrichments. Nothing kinetic / regulatory
is involved and the absolute scale of the culture, e.g. the maximal
bioreactor cell density, is irrelevant for the flux distribution per
C-mol biomass.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry – required. The stoichiometric
matrix S and the atom transition maps that underlie the isotopomer
balance equations are the model. Without S no mass balance can be written
and no labelling propagation can be defined.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates – required.
The experimental constraints for MFA are the measured 13C enrichments
of intracellular, or proteinogenic, metabolites, usually expressed as
mass isotopomer distributions or MID’s. The MID’s together with S give
the non-linear labelling balance equations that resolve the otherwise
underdetermined linear system S·v = 0.

Enzyme kinetics 4. and regulatory networks 5. are not used in a
steady-state MFA. The fluxes are obtained from stoichiometry plus
labelling constraints, not from v = f(E,Km,kcat) nor from gene
regulation. Maximum cell density 2. of the bioreactor is a scale
factor and is not a constraint for the relative flux distribution.

In practice the stoichiometric model is closed with a biomass
formation reaction. The coefficients of that drain are normally written
in terms of the macromolecular composition of the organism, i.e. the
fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. that makes up the biomass.
Hence biomass composition 3. is routinely required to define the
biomass sink that closes the carbon, redox and degree-of-reduction
balances and to convert a measured growth rate into a C-mol biomass
demand. With the biomass reaction included the routinely used inputs
are therefore 1, 3 and 6. If the biomass drain is taken as a generic
lumped sink the minimal, formally independent, inputs for 13C-MFA are
the stoichiometric network 1 and the measured 13C labelling patterns 6,
i.e. two items in the list.
public_text.11:
In a formal 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the stoichiometric
consequences of the network and from the measured mass isotopomer
distributions, under the steady state assumption dC/dt = 0 , dX/dt = 0.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry - yes.  The stoichiometric matrix
N v = 0 together with the atom transition mappings for every reaction
is the structural part of the model on which the isotopomer balances

    dX/dt = f(v,X) = 0

are written. Without a defined network the isotopomer balances cannot
be formulated.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates - yes.
The measured mass isotopomer distributions, e.g. of proteinogenic
amino acids / intracellular metabolites that are the experimental
read-out of the 13C-labelling experiment, are the data that constrain
the flux distribution v. The MFA problem is

    minimise || Xmeas - Xcalc(v) ||  s.t.  N v = 0 

so the labeling data are the essential experimental input.

The other items are not part of the steady state 13C-MFA formulation.

* 2. Maximum cell density in a bioreactor - not required.  Cell density
is a scale-up / bioprocess parameter. Fluxes are expressed in
mmol gDW-1 h-1 or specific rates and are independent of the absolute
biomass that can be reached in a bioreactor.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics - not required.  MFA is stoichiometric /
isotopomer based. Kinetic constants, Vmax/Km etc., are needed for
kinetic or dynamic flux modelling but not for a steady state
isotopomer based flux estimation.

* 5. Regulatory networks - not required.  Regulation can be used to
reduce the solution space a posteriori but it is not a formal
requirement for the 13C-MFA equations.

* 3. Biomass composition - not a formal requirement of the MFA
equations themselves.  It is routinely used in practice to write an
explicit biomass drain reaction and to close carbon/nitrogen balances
and to convert a measured growth rate into a specific biomass
formation flux.  In the strict stoichiometric + isotopomer formulation
the biomass sink can be introduced as a measured specific growth rate
with an unspecified composition.  If a fully closed network with an
explicit biomass reaction is required in practice the biomass
composition is the third practical input in addition to 1 and 6.

Hence from the list as written the formal, indispensable MFA inputs are
stoichiometry and the measured 13C labelling patterns, i.e. 2 of the 6
items, 1 and 6.  With the usual practical closure of the model the
biomass composition is also brought in, giving the commonly quoted
three practical inputs: stoichiometry, biomass composition and isotopic
labelling.
public_text.9:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained
by fitting an isotopomer / cumomer model to measured labeling data under
steady state mass balance constraints.

The core of the method is

* a defined metabolic network with atom mappings,
 i.e. the reaction stoichiometry and the carbon transitions which link
 substrate atoms to product atoms. The stoichiometry provides the
 mass balances 

    S . v =0

and the atom transitions which are used to build the isotopomer
balance equations. Kinetic parameters and the regulatory state of the
network are not entered in the isotopomer balance.

* the experimental 13C labeling pattern of the intracellular
metabolic intermediates, usually obtained by GC-MS / LC-MS/MS after
steady state labeling with [U-13C] glucose or other tracers, and the
corresponding extracellular flux rates which are used to scale the
model. The labeling data are the only experimentally observed
quantities which break the stoichiometric degree of freedom of the
network.

In particular maximum cell density in the bioreactor, enzyme
kinetics and the regulatory network are not used in steady state
13C-MFA. The maximum cell density is a process / scale up parameter
and kinetics / regulation are not required for a stoichiometric/
isotopomer fit.

In practice the network is closed with a biomass formation reaction.
Writing that reaction needs the macromolecular biomass composition,
protein/lipid/carbohydrate etc., i.e. the stoichiometric coefficients
of the precursors that are drained to growth. Once the biomass
reaction is written it is part of the stoichiometric model. Strictly
speaking the isotopomer fit therefore needs

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry,
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates,

and, in the usual implementation, the biomass stoichiometry which is
specified by 3. Biomass composition of the organism. Items 2. Maximum
cell density, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not
required for steady state 13C-MFA.

If the biomass reaction is taken as given within item 1 the minimal
information set is stoichiometry + labeling, i.e. two of the six listed
items, 1 and 6. With the conventional explicit biomass formulation this
is normally quoted as the three items 1, 3 and 6, 2, 4 and 5 being
unnecessary.
public_text.13:
3

For a steady-state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained from mass balance constraints plus the information contained in the measured isotopomers. That needs:

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, to write the atom mappings and the stoichiometric mass balance equations for each metabolite at steady state, dC/dt = 0.

6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, which are the experimental data that constrain the fractional contributions of different precursor pools to each metabolite and therefore the flux split ratios.

3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. fraction of protein, lipids and carbohydrates. The biomass drain must be represented as a pseudo-reaction in the network. Its stoichiometry, and therefore the carbon demand that closes the network, is defined by the measured biomass composition. Without a defined biomass reaction you cannot enforce carbon and redox closure and the labeling of the biomass precursors cannot be properly accounted for.

Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not required for the isotopic steady-state calculation. The fluxes are inferred from stoichiometry and isotopomer balancing, not from kinetic parameters, regulation or culture scale.
public_text.7:
3 items are required, namely 1, 3 and 6.

Stoichiometry is essential to build the atom transition matrix and the mass balance equations that define the network topology at steady state. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates are the experimental data that constrain the flux solution in 13C-MFA; without measured mass isotopomer distributions there is no way to resolve flux splits.

Biomass composition is also needed in practice to define a proper biomass drain reaction. In a steady-state 13C-MFA the network has to be closed and the carbon fate to biomass must be accounted for, which is done via a biomass equation constructed from the measured fractions of protein, lipids and carbohydrates and the corresponding average amino acid, fatty acid and sugar compositions. That closes the mass balance and allows conversion of relative fluxes to absolute fluxes. Maximum cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used for the stoichiometric + isotopomer balancing that underlies steady-state 13C-MFA.
public_text.3:
In a steady-state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the consistency of a
stoichiometric / atom-transition model with experimentally measured isotopomer
distributions. The kinetic / regulatory description of the network is not used
and the culture scale is not used.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry : required. The atom mapping of the
network, i.e. the reaction stoichiometry together with the carbon atom
transitions, is the structural model on which the isotopomer balances are
written. Without a defined network the labelling data cannot be mapped onto
flux ratios.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates : required.
The measured 13C enrichment of intracellular intermediates, in practice
usually of proteinogenic amino acids derived from the intracellular
metabolite pool, is the experimental constraint that makes the flux ratios
identifiable. Steady state 13C-MFA is the joint solution of
S.v = 0 and of the isotopomer balance equations
v → MID

* 4. Enzyme kinetics, 5. Regulatory networks and 2. Maximum cell density of
the organism in a bioreactor are not required for the isotopic
constraint based calculation. Steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric /
isotopomer method and is independent of kinetic parameters, regulation
and of the absolute scale of cultivation.

In practice absolute fluxes are obtained only after the isotopic flux
ratios are scaled to an absolute scale, e.g. by a measured specific growth
rate and a defined biomass formation reaction. The biomass formation
reaction is normally written from the measured biomass composition, i.e.
the fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc., so that the drain of
precursor metabolites to biomass can be closed in the stoichiometric model.
With the usual textbook complete model this is the third piece of
information that is used together with 1 and 6, i.e. stoichiometry +
biomass composition + labelling data.

If the scaling is taken as given the strictly isotopic essentials are the
two listed items 1 and 6, stoichiometry + measured 13C labelling patterns.
That is the 2-item core of 13C-MFA, routinely quoted as 3 items in the
practical implementation 1,3 and 6.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation round 0 shows strong consensus on the core of steady-state 13C-MFA and a split on how to count biomass composition.

Core agreement:
* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required. The stoichiometric matrix S v = 0 and the carbon atom transition / atom mapping for each reaction are needed to write mass balances and isotopomer/cumomer balance equations. The biomass formation reaction is part of the network description.
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates is required. Measured mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular / proteinogenic metabolites from a 13C tracer experiment at isotopic steady state are the experimental constraints that make flux ratios identifiable: min_v ||MID_meas - MID_pred(v)|| s.t. S v = 0.
* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor is not required. Fluxes are expressed per biomass / specific rates; absolute scale is set by measured uptake/secretion rates, not maximal density.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics is not required. 13C-MFA is stoichiometric/isotopomer based, not kinetic.
* 5. Regulatory networks is not required. Regulation is not part of the steady-state isotopomer balance formulation.

Disagreement / nuance on 3. Biomass composition of the organism:
* Formal/minimal view: Biomass can be left as an unspecified lumped drain or included generically in the stoichiometric model. Strictly indispensable inputs are then 1 and 6, i.e. 2 of the 6 listed items, stoichiometry + atom mapping and measured 13C labelling.
* Practical/closed network view: In routine implementations the network is closed with an explicit biomass drain reaction whose stoichiometric coefficients are built from measured fractional composition of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, RNA, DNA, etc. That defines carbon/R species demand and allows conversion of relative fluxes to absolute fluxes. In that conventional practice items 1, 3 and 6 are used, i.e. 3 of the 6 items, with 1 and 6 being the strictly isotopic essentials and 3 the practical closure.

Unresolved for final answer: whether the question asks for the formal mathematical minimum 2 items, 1+6, or the textbook practical set 3 items, 1+3+6. Most colleagues note both, with 1+3+6 being the commonly quoted practical requirement and 1+6 the irreducible formal core. Items 2,4,5 remain unnecessary in all accounts.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion converges on a core vs practical distinction for steady state 13C-MFA.

Core mathematical requirements are consistently identified as:
* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with carbon atom mapping. Needed for S·v = 0 mass balance and for building the isotopomer / cumomer balance equations that map fluxes to predicted labelling.
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Measured mass isotopomer distributions / 13C enrichments of intracellular or proteinogenic amino acid pools are the experimental constraints that make the flux distribution identifiable, together with known tracer input.

Unanimously not required:
* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor – process scale parameter, fluxes are per gDW/h; specific uptake/secretion rates are needed but max density is not.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics – 13C-MFA is stoichiometric/isotopomer, not kinetic.
* 5. Regulatory networks – not part of the steady state isotopomer balance.

    S·v = 0 ,   dX/dt = f(S,atom map,v)=0

and the flux vector is obtained by fitting the predicted mass
isotopomer / fractional labelling distributions to the measured ones.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, with the carbon atom
transitions for every reaction, is required.  S and the atom mapping
define the mass balances and the isotopomer balance equations
MIDcalc(v).  The biomass formation reaction is part of the
stoichiometric description of the network.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates is
required.  The measured 13C mass isotopomer distributions of the
intracellular pools, normally proteinogenic amino acids / free

extracellular tracer labelling is implied.

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism.  In the conventional closed
implementation the network is closed with an explicit biomass drain
reaction

    Biomass = Σi ci Mi

fractional macromolecular composition protein/lipid/carbohydrate/RNA/DNA
etc.  That defines the carbon, redox and degree-of-reduction demand
to growth and allows the measured specific growth rate / extracellular
exchange rates to be expressed in C-mol biomass h-1 and absolute

explicitly the routinely quoted practical data set for a closed

Items 2,4 and 5 are not part of the steady state isotopomer
formulation.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No. Fluxes

absolute scale of the culture is irrelevant for the flux distribution.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No. 13C-MFA is stoichiometric/isotopomer, not

bound fluxes but it is not a formal requirement for the S·v=0 and

A workable steady-state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric + isotopomer problem, but it is a closed network problem.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required. The stoichiometric matrix S and the carbon atom transitions for each reaction define S·v = 0 and the mapping v → predicted mass isotopomer distributions. Without a defined network you cannot write the isotopomer balances.

6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates is required. The measured 13C mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular pools, normally proteinogenic amino acids as proxies for central carbon intermediates, are the experimental constraints that make the flux ratios identifiable. Together with the atom mapping they give the non-linear fit min_v || MID_meas – MID_calc(v) ||.

3. Biomass composition of the organism is also required in practice to close the model. Item 1 as listed is the metabolic reaction stoichiometry, not the biomass drain. The biomass formation/drain pseudo-reaction that closes carbon, redox and degree-of-reduction balances is written from the measured fractional amounts of protein, lipid, carbohydrate, RNA, DNA etc. That composition gives the molar demand for precursors per C-mol biomass and allows the measured growth rate / specific uptake rates to be converted into absolute intracellular fluxes and to account for label loss into biomass. Without a defined biomass composition the network is open, carbon is unaccounted for, and you cannot anchor the relative flux ratios obtained from the isotopomer fit to an absolute scale.

Items 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in the steady-state isotopomer formulation. The method is stoichiometric/isotopomer based, scale independent and kinetic free.

So from the six items listed the practical inputs that are routinely needed for a closed, interpretable steady-state 13C-MFA are stoichiometry, a defined biomass drain built from biomass composition, and the measured 13C labeling patterns: items 1, 3 and 6, i.e. three of the six items. Formally the biomass reaction can be absorbed into the stoichiometric description, which is why the strictly mathematical core is often quoted as 1+6, but as separate listed inputs the closed model needs 1+3+6.

Steady-state 13C-MFA is the joint solution of

S v = 0
dX/dt = 0

with the flux vector obtained from min_v || MIDmeas – MIDcalc(v,S,atom map)|| s.t. S v = 0.

That is a stoichiometric / isotopomer constraint problem, kinetic free and regulatory free.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with carbon atom transitions / atom mapping. Required. S and the atom transition network define Sv = 0 and the isotopomer / cumomer balances that map a flux vector v to a predicted 13C labelling. * 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Required. Biomass = Σ ci Mi

whose stoichiometric coefficients ci are built from an independent experimental measurement of the fractional macromolecular composition protein / lipid / carbohydrate / RNA / DNA etc. That composition closes C/N/redox/degree-of-reduction balances, defines the precursor demand to growth, accounts for label loss to biomass and allows anchoring of the relative flux ratios from the MID fit to absolute fluxes mmol gDW-1 h-1 via the measured growth / exchange rates.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry + atom mapping
3. Biomass composition to define the biomass drain and close the network
6. Measured 13C isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates

i.e. three of the six listed items, 2, 4 and 5 remaining unnecessary.

Formally the isotopomer equations can be written with a lumped, externally measured biomass sink so that the mathematically irreducible core from the list is 1 + 6, two listed items, with the biomass reaction then absorbed in the stoichiometric description in 1.
